lesson.title: The United States Enters World War I
lesson.subject: social-studies

contentBlocks.text: Last week you studied the Progressive Era's reforms. This week: America's entry onto the world stage in World War I!

The United States initially stayed neutral when World War I began in Europe in 1914, but entered the war in 1917, driven by several factors including German submarine attacks on ships (including some carrying Americans) and a general shift in public opinion toward supporting the Allied powers. This marked a significant change from America's earlier, more isolated foreign policy. Explain why German attacks on ships carrying Americans would have been a significant factor in shifting US public opinion toward joining the war.
You just learned why the US entered World War I! Tomorrow we'll see how the war's end reshaped America's role in the world.

objectives: State the basic timeline and key factor (submarine attacks) in the US decision to enter WWI
Explain why attacks on American lives shifted public opinion toward war
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's Progressive Era work briefly.
2. Introduce the US's initial neutrality and 1917 entry into WWI.
3. Have the child explain the submarine-attacks factor.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's war's-end lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple cause-and-effect framing — an attack that harms your own citizens is a direct, personal reason for a country to reconsider staying uninvolved
Ready for more: ask the child why a country might prefer to stay neutral in a conflict for as long as possible before that changes
Kept at a general historical-overview level, appropriate for opening this week's chronological continuation from last week's Progressive Era
teacherGuide.answerKey: Attacks that harmed or killed American citizens made the war feel much more direct and personal to the American public, rather than a distant conflict between other countries — this kind of direct harm is a powerful factor in shifting public and political opinion toward involvement, since it changes the war from something happening 'over there' to something with real consequences at home.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses WA Social Studies and C3 Framework History standards on early 20th-century US foreign policy, opening this week's thread as a chronological continuation of last week's Progressive Era unit.
